before: A custom hook is a function that uses React hooks to package reusable stateful behavior. Its name begins with use.
Call custom hooks at the top level of a component or another hook. Do not call them conditionally or inside an event handler.
A hook can return an object containing its current value and actions. A component chooses how to display and trigger those actions.
For the exercise, useCounter(initial) returns count, increment, and reset. Both counters start at 2. Incrementing A must not change B; resetting A returns only A to its initial value.
after: A custom Hook is a function that uses React Hooks to share reusable behavior. Its name starts with `use`. Components can use the same logic without sharing one stored value.
Each call to the Hook has its own state. The initial value sets the starting state; changing that argument later does not automatically restart the state.
Call Hooks at the top of a component or another Hook. Keep them outside conditions, loops, and event handlers so React can track them in the same order.
A Hook may return an object with a value and action functions. The component decides how to show the value and which buttons call the actions.

Complete `useCounter(initial)` to return `count`, `increment`, and `reset`. Both counters start at 2. Changing A must leave B alone. Reset is a separate action that sets this counter to the initial argument supplied in the current render.

before.question: Two components call the same useCounter hook. Why does clicking one not change the other?
choices: Each hook call has its own state associated with its component
The hook is copied into a separate JavaScript file each time
before.explanation: A custom hook reuses the stateful logic. Its calls use independent React state; shared state would need an explicit common owner or store.

after.question: Why does clicking one counter not change another that uses the same Hook?
choices: Each Hook call has its own React state.
React creates a separate JavaScript file each time.
after.explanation: The definition shares the instructions. Each call keeps its own state.

changes.before: The initial argument is stable in this exercise; changing it later does not reinitialize useState automatically. No effect needed. Custom hooks must obey the same top-level call rules as built-in hooks.
changes.after: Changing the initial argument does not restart useState. The reset action explicitly uses the initial argument from its current render.

project.title: Reuse state logic with a custom hook
